prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Late winter, almost spring. It's like finding a diamond; now I don't want to leave. I sit in the dirt and put my hands in your tracks. For the first time in a long time I don't doubt. Now I know I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of disclosure, the long-felt presence Suddenly incarnate. Behind me my friend warns, If we see the bear, get into a fetal position. No problem, I tell her, I'm always in a fetal position—I was born in a fetal position. Did you know, she says, the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like a human man? I skip a stone, feel a sudden bloat of grief, then laugh. I ask her, Who would shave a bear? We climb Farther up Rattlesnake Creek, watch winter sun glitter off dark water. No matter how high we go I look higher. Sometimes absence can prove presence. That's not exactly faith, I know. All day, everywhere, I feel you near at hand. There's so much to understand, and everything to prove. Up high the air is thin and hard, roars in the ears like love.

Keywords: Late, For, Now

outputs.L1:
Late winter, on the very cusp of spring. It feels like unearthing a diamond; now I have no wish to leave. I settle into the dirt and press my hands into your tracks. For the first time in a long while, I am free of doubt. Now I understand that I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of revelation, the long-felt presence suddenly made flesh.

Behind me, my friend cautions, *If we see the bear, curl into a fetal position.* No trouble at all, I tell her—I am always in a fetal position; I was born in one. *Did you know,* she says, *that the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like that of a human man?* I skip a stone across the water, feel a sudden swell of grief, then laugh. I ask her, *Who would ever shave a bear?*

We climb farther up Rattlesnake Creek and watch the winter sun glitter off the dark water. No matter how high we ascend, I find myself looking higher still. Sometimes absence can affirm presence. That is not quite faith, I know. All day, everywhere, I feel you close at hand. There is so much to comprehend, and everything left to prove. Up high, the air grows thin and sharp, roaring in the ears like love.
outputs.L2: The tail end of winter, spring nearly here. The feeling resembles unearthing a gem; leaving is the last thing I want now. I lower myself onto the ground and press my palms into your footprints. After so long, my uncertainty has vanished. It's clear to me now that some part of me always sensed you here. You mark where revelation starts, that presence I've sensed forever, all at once made flesh. Behind me, my companion cautions that should the bear appear, I should curl up tight. That's easy, I answer—I'm forever curled up tight; I came into the world that way. Then she asks whether I realized that a bear stripped of its fur has a body identical to a man's. I send a stone skimming across the surface, feel a swelling wave of sorrow rise up, and then break into laughter. I wonder aloud who on earth would ever shave a bear. We keep going, ascending along Rattlesnake Creek, and observe the pale winter light shimmering across the shadowed water. However far we ascend, my gaze keeps reaching beyond. At times, what's missing can testify to what's there. I understand that isn't precisely the same as belief. Throughout the entire day, in every direction, I sense you close by. So much remains to grasp, and nothing has yet been confirmed. At this altitude the air turns sparse and severe, thundering in my ears the way love does.

# Tracks in the Dirt

Sitting in the dirt among the tracks, the speaker is overtaken by a profound moment of certainty and connection. There, with the earth beneath and the impressions of passage all around, something long-anticipated finally becomes real—a presence that had lived only in imagination and hope now takes on solid form. It is a quiet revelation, arriving not with fanfare but with the settled weight of knowing, as though the ground itself confirms what the heart has waited to believe.

Woven into this experience is a conversation with a friend about bears, a exchange that carries both humor and unease. The banter is lighthearted on its surface, the easy talk of companions, yet beneath it runs a current of tension—the acknowledgment of real danger, and with it, an intimation of grief. In this blending of laughter and dread, the poem captures how joy and fear often travel together, how the presence of something wild can delight and threaten in the same breath.

As they climb higher along Rattlesnake Creek, the speaker's gaze keeps drifting past each new height. No summit satisfies; every rise reveals another beyond it, and the eyes continue searching. This restless looking suggests a longing that cannot be fulfilled by arrival, an unending pursuit of something greater than any single vantage can provide. The physical ascent becomes a mirror of an inner striving that refuses to rest.

From this striving emerges a paradox the speaker turns over carefully: that absence itself can serve as evidence of presence. What is missing, what cannot be seen or grasped, becomes its own kind of proof—a sign pointing toward the very thing it lacks. The speaker recognizes that this belief comes close to faith, though it stops just short of it, hovering at the threshold between conviction and doubt, unwilling or unable to make the final leap.

The poem closes in the thin, harsh air of the high mountains, where breath comes hard and the atmosphere seems to roar like love. Here the physical struggle of the climb fuses with an overwhelming emotional and spiritual longing, the difficulty of simply breathing transformed into a sound as vast and consuming as devotion itself. In that final image, body and spirit become one, and the ache of the ascent gives voice to a yearning that surpasses words.
outputs.L4:
# Along Rattlesnake Creek

The poem opens in the transitional season of late winter, when the ground still holds the memory of cold but has begun to soften. The speaker walks along Rattlesnake Creek, following its course through a landscape that is neither fully frozen nor fully thawed—a fitting metaphor for the state of belief the poem will come to explore. The water moves alongside the speaker's steps, a companion that is both constant and always passing.

Early in the walk, the speaker notices animal tracks pressed into the mud and remaining snow. These marks become the poem's first meditation on presence and absence. The tracks are evidence of creatures that are no longer there—proof of passage rather than of the animal itself. Here the speaker begins to sense a paradox that will deepen throughout the poem: that we most often know things not by seeing them directly, but by the impressions they leave behind. The bear, imagined or evidenced somewhere in the wilderness, becomes a presence felt precisely because it remains unseen, its nearness suggested by claw marks, disturbed earth, or simply the charged quality of the air.

As the speaker climbs, the physical ascent up the mountainside mirrors an inner movement. The body's effort—the burning muscles, the labored breath, the deliberate placing of one foot above the other—grounds the poem's spiritual searching in something tangible and real. This is not abstract theology but faith worked out through the flesh, through exertion and attention.

Woven through the hike are moments of raw human feeling. Grief surfaces unexpectedly, perhaps for someone absent or lost, the emotion rising like the creek's cold current. Yet laughter comes too, sudden and unbidden, breaking through the solemnity. These oscillations between sorrow and joy reflect the unpredictable texture of a life lived in relationship with the unseen—a life that cannot rest in easy certainty but moves instead through swells of doubt and moments of unexpected grace.

The poem builds toward its central paradox: that absence can prove presence. Just as the tracks confirm the animal that made them, just as the empty space at a table testifies to the one who is gone, the speaker comes to understand that what is missing can be its own kind of evidence. Spiritual conviction, the poem suggests, does not arise from proof or from clear sight. It emerges instead from the felt experience of something near yet unseen—a nearness sensed in the body, in the wilderness, in the very ache of not being able to see.

By the poem's close, the speaker has arrived at a hard-won and paradoxical faith. It is not the faith of answers or of visible presence, but of trust in what can only be felt: the conviction that the unseen is real precisely because we feel its nearness, because it leaves its mark on us, because its absence carves a shape that testifies to what was and is and might yet be there.
outputs.L5:
# Better Late Than Never

We've all heard the saying "better late than never," and while there's truth to it, timing matters more than we often admit.

Being **late** is something everyone experiences. Whether it's arriving late to a meeting, submitting an assignment past the deadline, or realizing you've delayed an important conversation for too long, lateness carries consequences. Yet it also teaches us valuable lessons about planning, respect for others' time, and the importance of preparation.

But here's the thing: it's never too late to change. If you've been putting something off, this moment—right **now**—is the perfect time to begin. The past cannot be rewritten, but the present belongs entirely to you.

So what have you been waiting **for**? Perhaps you've been searching for the ideal conditions, the perfect opportunity, or a guarantee of success before taking that first step. The truth is, waiting for perfection often becomes an excuse for inaction.

## The Power of Now

The present moment is all we truly have. Yesterday is gone, and tomorrow remains uncertain. When we focus on **now**, we reclaim our power to act. Instead of dwelling on how late we are or making excuses for our delays, we can channel that energy into meaningful progress.

Consider these simple truths:

- It's never too **late** to learn a new skill
- The best time to start is **now**, not tomorrow
- Whatever you're waiting **for** may never arrive on its own

## Taking the First Step

Don't let the fear of being late stop you from starting at all. Every expert was once a beginner. Every success story began with someone who decided that now was the right time to act.

So take that step. Make that call. Start that project. Because the perfect moment you've been waiting for is already here—it's happening right now.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about searching for a bear in early spring near a creek, addressing the bear as "you" throughout.
counterfactuals.output:
# Waking Ground

I come looking for you
where the snowmelt runs loud,
where the creek has thrown off its winter glass
and speaks again in the old language.

The alders are still bare fingers.
I read the mud for you—
that wide palm pressed into the bank,
five moons of claw
walking away from me.

You are somewhere in this thawing dark,
lean from the long sleep,
your ribs a ladder under the loose coat,
your hunger simple as the creek's hunger
to reach the sea.

I turn the winter-flattened logs
the way you would,
looking for the pale grubs,
the first green shoots
you'd pull with your soft blunt mouth.

I don't want to find you, exactly.
I want to know you passed through—
that you climbed out of the ground
another year,
that the mountain still holds
one animal larger than my fear of it.

The willows redden.
Somewhere your breath is fogging
in a slant of first sun.
Somewhere you shake the cold from your fur
and the water beads fall
like the last of the snow letting go.

I leave before dusk,
before the hour you come down to drink.
I leave you the creek,
the mud,
the whole unfolding season—

and carry out only this:
the print I did not touch,
filling slowly
with clear rising water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative poem that blends faith, doubt, and the search for presence, set during a hike in late winter.
counterfactuals.output:
# Late Winter Ascent

I climbed because the house had grown too quiet,
because the questions there had learned my name
and followed me from room to room like weather.

The trail was neither frozen now nor thawed—
that undecided season, mud and ice,
the snow retreating into shaded folds
the way belief withdraws but does not leave.

I used to pray the way I used to breathe,
unthinking, certain of the air.
Now every word feels borrowed, held too long,
a coin worn smooth of its imprinted face.

And yet I climbed. And yet the birches held
their silver silence like a kind of psalm
I could not read but somehow leaned against.

Is doubt the absence, or the shape
that longing takes when it outgrows its answers?
I do not know. I know the cold stream ran
beneath its lid of ice, still speaking, still
insisting on its downhill argument.

Near the ridge I stopped. The wind came through
and moved the bare trees into something like
a gesture—reaching, or perhaps release.
I waited for a voice. None came.

But waiting, I grew still enough to hear
the small particulars: my own rough breath,
a chickadee, the creak of leaning wood,
the sun's faint warmth arriving on my face
like a hand laid gently on a fevered child.

Maybe presence isn't what descends
in fire or certainty or thunderclap.
Maybe it is the world, insisting quietly
that I am in it—that I have not left,
that even doubt is a form of attention,
a way of keeping watch beside the door.

I turned toward home. The light was going soft.
I did not find what I had come to find.
I found instead the finding was the path,
the ice, the mud, the undecided ground—

and something walking with me, or ahead,
that left no print, but bent the grass a little,
and did not answer, and did not depart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem where the speaker follows animal tracks and reflects on absence proving presence, including a humorous exchange with a friend about bears.
counterfactuals.output:
# Tracks

I found them near the frozen creek this morning—
five-toed, deliberate, pressed into the mud
like punctuation in a sentence
I arrived too late to read.

Something walked here.
Something breathed this air, shook frost
from its shoulders, went on
about the business of being alive
while I was somewhere else, asleep,
dreaming of nothing worth remembering.

This is the strange arithmetic of woods:
the emptiness itself becomes the proof.
No creature in sight, yet everywhere
the evidence of creatures—
the bent grass, the scattered seed,
the hollow where a body warmed the ground.

Absence, it turns out,
is just presence wearing a disguise.

I texted my friend a photo.
*Bear?* I asked, thrilled, already
composing the heroic version.

*That's a dog,* she wrote back.
*Probably a Labrador.*

*It could be a bear,* I insisted.

*Was there a leash?*

*Bears don't wear leashes.*

*There's a leash in the picture, genius.*

And there was—red nylon,
curling at the edge of the frame
like a small embarrassment.

So: no bear.
Only Winston, or Duke, or Bella,
hauling some neighbor down the trail
toward breakfast.

And yet I stood there longer than I should have,
grateful for the lesson twice delivered:
that the world is thick with things
just out of sight,

that what we cannot see
still leaves its mark on us,

and that a friend who calls you *genius*
means it, mostly,
the way the mud means *paw,*
the way the empty trail
still means somebody, somewhere,
went walking on ahead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, meditative poem set along Rattlesnake Creek that explores longing, faith, and connection to something wild and unseen.
counterfactuals.output:
# Along Rattlesnake Creek

Here where the water learns to speak
in syllables of stone and light,
I come with all my emptiness
to kneel beside the running white.

The pines lean close as if to hear
some confession I can't make—
how longing is a kind of prayer
addressed to nothing for its sake.

I've followed faith like following
a current toward its hidden source,
believing that the wild knows how
to bear a body's slow divorce

from certainty. The willows bend.
The mayflies rise in golden thirst.
And something moves along the bank
that was here long before the first

soft word for God was ever spoken—
older than the name for want,
more patient than the human need
to find the sacred, and to haunt

these waters looking for a face
in every ripple, every gleam.
I cup the cold into my hands.
It slips away like every dream

of holding what was never mine.
And yet I stay. The evening cools.
The creek continues, unconcerned,
obeying only its own rules—

which may be grace, or may be just
the way that wildness lets us near
without belonging, without keys,
the way the unseen holds us here:

not answered, but accompanied.
Not filled, but somehow less alone.
The rattlesnake sun coils down.
The dark comes soft as flesh on bone,

and still the water speaks, and speaks,
a language I will never learn—
and this is faith: to love the voice
and ask for nothing in return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person narrative poem about hiking, spirituality, and a strange conversation about what a shaved bear looks like.
counterfactuals.output:
# Trail Companions

I set out at the pale edge of morning,
boots laced against the mountain's stony face,
seeking that old wordless thing—
the way the light comes slantwise through the pines
and something in me quiets,
something I've been calling God
for lack of a better name.

My friend walked ahead, breath fogging,
and I was deep in reverence,
watching how the mist rose off the ridge
like prayer made visible,
when he turned and said,
"You ever wonder what a bear looks like shaved?"

I stopped.

The cathedral of the morning
did not collapse,
but tilted,
the way a held note bends.

"Like a very muscular man," he said,
"who lost a bet with God.
All that dignity in the face,
and underneath—
just a sad, pink, overgrown dog.
Loose skin. Terrible posture.
The saddest thing you'd ever see."

And I laughed,
and the laugh went up the mountain
same as any hymn,
scattering the small birds from the brush,
and I thought—

maybe this is it, too.
Not just the light, the silence,
the great cold breathing of the trees,
but this:
a friend beside me on the switchbacks,
saying something so magnificently stupid
that the whole hushed world leans in
to overhear.

We climbed.
The summit waited, patient as always.
And somewhere in the valley
a bear went about its holy business,
gloriously unshaved,
never once suspecting
it had wandered
into someone's idea of the divine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
